what_its_for: Tigecycline is an antibiotic used to treat certain serious bacterial infections, including skin and soft tissue infections, abdominal (belly) infections, and a type of pneumonia (lung infection) called community-acquired pneumonia. It works by stopping bacteria from growing and spreading in your body.
how_to_take: Tigecycline is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it is slowly injected into a vein through a needle or catheter. A healthcare provider (nurse or doctor) will give you this medication, usually in a hospital or clinic setting. Each infusion is given over about 30 to 60 minutes. Do not try to give yourself this medication at home unless specifically trained and instructed by your healthcare team.
dosing: The usual starting dose is 100 mg given one time into your vein. After that, you will receive 50 mg every 12 hours (twice a day). Your doctor will decide exactly how long your treatment lasts, which is usually 5 to 14 days depending on your infection. If you have liver problems, your doctor may give you a lower dose. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
missed_dose: Because this medication is given by a healthcare provider in a medical setting, a missed dose is unlikely. However, if you miss a scheduled appointment or infusion, contact your doctor or clinic right away to reschedule as soon as possible. Do not try to double up on doses to make up for a missed one.
storage: Tigecycline is stored and prepared by healthcare professionals. Unopened vials should be stored at room temperature (around 68°F to 77°F / 20°C to 25°C). Once mixed for infusion, the solution should be used within a certain time frame as directed by your pharmacist or healthcare team. Keep it out of direct light and away from heat.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor about ALL medications you take, including vitamins and supplements, before starting this antibiotic. Avoid taking blood thinners like warfarin (Coumadin) without close monitoring, as tigecycline may increase your risk of bleeding. Avoid becoming pregnant during treatment, as tigecycline can harm an unborn baby. Do not breastfeed while receiving this medication without first talking to your doctor. Avoid prolonged sun or UV light exposure, as this drug may make your skin more sensitive to sunburn.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency help if you experience: severe allergic reaction (rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, difficulty breathing); severe or watery diarrhea that does not stop (this could be a dangerous bowel infection called C. difficile); signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), dark urine, or severe stomach pain; unusual bruising or bleeding; severe nausea or vomiting; signs of pancreatitis such as severe upper stomach pain spreading to your back; or any new or worsening symptoms during treatment.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within a few days of starting tigecycline, but it is very important to complete the full course of treatment even if you feel better. Stopping the antibiotic too early can allow the infection to come back and become harder to treat. Most infections treated with tigecycline improve within 5 to 14 days.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Tigecycline should NOT be used during pregnancy, especially during the second and third trimesters, because it can harm the developing baby (including effects on bone and tooth development). Tell your doctor immediately if you become pregnant. Breastfeeding: It is not known if tigecycline passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: This medication is generally not recommended for children under 8 years of age, and use in children under 18 is limited. Older adults (65+): Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects; your doctor will monitor you closely. Liver disease: If you have severe liver disease, your doctor will reduce your dose to prevent harmful drug buildup in your body.
